title: "show us the straight path"
hook: "show us the straight path" — the whole prayer is a request for directions

segments.voice: Yesterday: mercy twice before anything else. The two mercy names came back before the word judgment ever appeared. Did you find two kind things to say before you judged something? Day eight.

Think about the last time you were properly lost. Not a little turned around. Lost. The phone at two percent, the street signs in a language you don't read, every corner looking like the one before. What did you finally do? You stopped someone and asked. Which way? It's a humbling question. It admits you don't know. Here's the surprise at the center of the prayer Muslims say most. Four verses of praise and mercy and trust, and then, when it finally asks for something, it doesn't ask for money, or health, or even forgiveness. It asks for directions.
screen: `PROPERLY LOST.` → `YOU STOP SOMEONE AND ASK.` → `THE PRAYER ASKS FOR DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the hinge of al-Fatiha, verse five, in Pickthall's words: “Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help.” Up to now the prayer has been talking about God. Here it turns and talks to God. Remember the conversation from yesterday, the hadith in Muslim where God answers each line? At this verse the answer changes: this part is between Me and My servant, and My servant will have what he asks. And what's asked comes next. “Show us the straight path.” The Arabic is ihdina s-sirata l-mustaqim. Ihdina comes from the root h-d-y, guidance, the same root as hidaya, and as a hadiya, a gift. Guidance, in this language, is something handed to you. Sirat is a road, a wide, clear way. Mustaqim: straight, standing upright, not bending. Notice the small word: us. Even someone praying completely alone, at three in the morning, says show us. Nobody asks for the road just for themselves. Then the last verse describes the road by its travelers: “The path of those whom Thou hast favoured.” And it names two ways of missing it: those who earn anger, and those who go astray. Commentators have read those two in more than one way. One common reading hears two kinds of lost: knowing the way and walking off it, and never finding it at all. And one more surprise. Muslims who pray the five prayers ask for this at least seventeen times a day. Even people who've prayed for fifty years. Scholars say that's the point: the path isn't found once. You ask for it again at every corner.
screen: `VERSE FIVE: THE PRAYER TURNS.` · `IHDINA — GUIDANCE, LIKE A GIFT.` · `EVEN ALONE, IT SAYS US.` · `ASKED AGAIN AT EVERY CORNER.` · then, large: `SHOW US THE STRAIGHT PATH.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about forty-five seconds. Sit comfortably. Think of one place in your life where you honestly don't know which way to go. A decision, a relationship, a next step. Don't solve it. Just stand at that corner for a moment and admit you don't know. If you pray, you can carry the line in Arabic or English: show us the straight path. If you don't, just hold the question open, like a hand. The bell holds the time.
Al-Fatiha, line three. Thee alone we worship, Thee alone we ask for help; show us the straight path. The request at the heart of the opening. Eighth word.
Your line: show me the way. Today, ask someone for directions you'd usually pretend you don't need. A coworker, a friend, a map. Notice how it feels to ask. Day eight.

howItsDone: Muslims recite al-Fatiha in Arabic at the start of every unit of every prayer, so the request for the straight path is said at least seventeen times a day; most Sunni Muslims then say amin.

original.note: Arabic: "guide us to the straight path." ihdina shares its root with hadiya, a gift.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about staying on the straight and narrow.
what it means: show us the straight path — the one request at the heart of the opening, asked for everyone, even when praying alone.

what a scholar hears: ihdina, from h-d-y, guidance as something given; sirat, a wide road; mustaqim, upright. the verse is prayed at least seventeen times a day because the path is asked for again, not found once.

notes: This day covers verses 5–7 (Kufan numbering), so verse 5 gets its place (see day 6's note). The index calls it 'line 3'.

Pickthall 1:5–7 quoted from memory: 'Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help. Show us the straight path, The path of those whom Thou hast favoured; Not (the path) of those who earn Thine anger nor of those who go astray.' Please confirm exact wording and punctuation.

The two groups in 1:7: a hadith (Tirmidhi 2954) and many commentators identify them with particular communities. The script gives only a common general reading (knowing the way and leaving it / never finding it) and says commentators read it in more than one way. A Keeper should decide whether this is the right level.
Hadith qudsi (Muslim 395): paraphrased; 'between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asked' at verse 5. Confirm.
h-d-y root: hidaya (guidance) and hadiya (gift) are generally given as the same root; confirm.

'At least seventeen times a day' refers to the seventeen required units; travelers shortening prayers recite fewer. Amin: said by most Sunni Muslims after al-Fatiha; Ja'fari Shia do not say it in prayer.
The carry 'show me the way' is singular while the verse says 'us'; the script leans into that difference in the teach. A Keeper may prefer the carry changed to 'show us the way' (an index edit).
